We've seen multiple examples showing that giving Meta's Muse app full disk access on Mac is a terrible idea, and now another major privacy issue has surfaced. The latest discovery reveals that Muse analyzes your communication records with everyone in your life every hour.

Apple's concern about this development is understandable. The company stated in a blog post that it will introduce additional controls for the "Full Disk Access" feature—the very feature that caused this problem……

Meta Muse app makes the situation urgent

Meta recently launched its Muse personal AI agent for iPhone and Mac. Despite it being obviously unwise to give a Meta app full access to all data on an Apple device, the app quickly rose to the top of the App Store charts.

Unsurprisingly, disaster soon followed. Wired reported that security researcher Karan Joshi discovered that Meta had instructed Muse to extract all the information needed to build a complete map of all your relationships—a situation that has yet to improve.

One of Muse's instructions appears to be the ability to "create a dedicated page for every person in the user's life." The instruction states that this hourly process consolidates data about family members, partners, friends, colleagues, "partners," and people you "follow." The instruction also reads: "Where they live, what they do for work, recurring topics (moving, shared savings goals)." The instruction further adds that the model can record "important dates," such as birthdays or anniversaries. A person's history file might include background details like "the trip in March, the argument that was eventually resolved, last week's milestone."

Apple tightens controls on Full Disk Access

You might assume that the prompt for granting an app "Full Disk Access" on Mac is self-explanatory, but that doesn't seem to be the case. Even tech-savvy users casually issue this all-access pass to their computers without realizing how dangerous this step is.

Apple says this feature was originally intended for backup applications, but developers have since used it for more purposes, including AI agents. The company said it plans to "introduce additional controls" to ensure users fully understand what they are doing when granting this permission.

Here's what Apple must do—and absolutely must not do

Apple says taking this step is "critical," and I completely agree. Since the current permission requests don't adequately convey the gravity of granting this access, Apple must ensure users truly understand what they're allowing.

What I'd like to see is clearer text reminding users that unless they are certain they understand the consequences, they should not proceed. Something along the lines of:

Basically, the wording cannot be too strong. For apps that have already been granted this permission, a one-time confirmation would also be welcome.

Top comment posted by Rayz2023

Do you really think the kind of person who would grant a Meta app disk-level access is the type who would willingly read more than two lines of text at once?

However, Apple must not repeat the mistake it made with screen recording in macOS Sequoia. Granted, that's equally dangerous, and issuing a stern warning is reasonable, but Apple's approach at the time was to force us to reconfirm these permissions every week and every time we restarted.

This move was widely criticized as turning macOS into Microsoft Vista and charging users "a subscription fee you didn't purchase and can't cancel." In my view, Apple's occasional prompts on iPhone to reconfirm permissions are already excessive. For example, I've already granted Citymapper access to my location so it can continue providing navigation in the background—so, Apple, I really don't need you to confirm again whether I still want this permission.

Yes, issue the sternest possible warning about granting Full Disk Access, but if someone chooses to do so, macOS must respect their decision. Thanks for the concern, but no mandatory confirmations—whether weekly or at any other interval.
